plan.contextChunk: This figure places two particle-packing diagrams side by side, each a flat array of identical teal spheres shaded to look rounded and drawn to fill a roughly square block. The left array, labeled Crystalline beneath it, has its spheres seated in straight horizontal rows stacked in a regular offset pattern, every sphere in contact with its neighbors so that the same local arrangement repeats throughout the block and continuous rows and diagonals can be traced from edge to edge. The right array, labeled Amorphous, holds spheres of the same size and color but set down with no repeating order: neighbor spacings vary, some particles nearly touch while irregular empty gaps open elsewhere, and no row or column runs through the block. Nothing else appears in either panel, no axes, container, or individually labeled particle, so the single visual variable is the arrangement of the spheres and the comparison asked of the reader is long-range order against its absence at similar overall density. The pairing illustrates the structural difference between solids whose atoms, ions, or molecules occupy a definite repeating pattern and noncrystalline or glassy solids that freeze before any ordered internal structure develops.

demo_steps.title: Compare the packings
demo_steps.narration: Both panels show similar particles at roughly similar density. The key difference is not particle type, but whether their positions repeat in a regular pattern.

demo_steps.title: Reveal long-range order
demo_steps.narration: Turn on the lattice guides: rows and diagonal paths run continuously through the crystalline block, but no comparable guide pattern fits the amorphous block.

demo_steps.title: Inspect a local neighborhood
demo_steps.narration: Click particles in each panel. In the crystal, neighboring particles appear at repeated distances and directions; in the amorphous solid, the nearest-neighbor pattern changes from place to place.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Crystalline and amorphous solids can contain the same kinds of particles, but only a crystal preserves a repeating arrangement over long distances.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Create two side-by-side particle blocks on a white background. Use identical teal spheres with radial shading or highlights to suggest rounded particles. The left block should be a dense, regular offset packing with clean horizontal rows and diagonal alignments that can be traced from edge to edge; label it 'Crystalline' beneath. The right block should occupy a similar rectangular area and density but place the same spheres irregularly, with varied nearest-neighbor distances and uneven gaps; label it 'Amorphous' beneath. The lattice guide toggle should draw subtle light lines or center-to-center paths only over the crystalline panel, not force a grid onto the amorphous panel. The click highlight should work in both panels by outlining the selected sphere, emphasizing nearby spheres, and drawing one or more translucent distance rings to compare repeated versus variable neighborhoods.

authoredContext:
When most liquids are cooled, they eventually freeze and form crystalline solids, solids in which the atoms, ions, or molecules are arranged in a definite repeating pattern. It is also possible for a liquid to freeze before its molecules become arranged in an orderly pattern. The resulting materials are called amorphous solids or noncrystalline solids (or, sometimes, glasses). The particles of such solids lack an ordered internal structure and are randomly arranged (the figure).

The entities of a solid phase may be arranged in a regular, repeating pattern (crystalline solids) or randomly (amorphous).

Two images are shown and labeled, from left to right, “Crystalline” and “Amorphous.” The crystalline diagram shows many circles drawn in rows and stacked together tightly. The amorphous diagram shows many circles spread slightly apart and in no organized pattern.

Metals and ionic compounds typically form ordered, crystalline solids. Substances that consist of large molecules, or a mixture of molecules whose movements are more restricted, often form amorphous solids. For examples, candle waxes are amorphous solids composed of large hydrocarbon molecules. Some substances, such as silicon dioxide (shown in the figure), can form either crystalline or amorphous solids, depending on the conditions under which it is produced. Also, amorphous solids may undergo a transition to the crystalline state under appropriate conditions.

discrepancies: The amorphous panel is noticeably more row-and-column aligned than the source; several particles sit on repeated horizontal/vertical bands, making it look less randomly packed.
The amorphous cluster has larger open gaps and a slightly different outer silhouette than the source, which appears more uniformly dense and irregular.
Some right-panel particles are pushed very close to the figure edge compared with the source, making the amorphous group feel wider and less balanced.
The generated sphere shading is close but somewhat more glossy/high-contrast than the softer teal spheres in the source.
evaluation.notes: The figure is clearly recognizable with correct labels and a strong crystalline/amorphous contrast, but the amorphous packing should be more irregular and closer in density to the source.
